verses.1: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, defines kawthar, on the fawʿal pattern, as something marked by abundance, hence abundant good. It reports readings including a stream or fountain in paradise, the Prophet’s children, his followers, scholars, the Qur’an and its ease, prophethood, Islam, tawḥīd, knowledge and wisdom, his merits, the praiseworthy station (17:79), and light in his heart—perhaps as many as twenty-six. It says only the first two derive from narrations and treats the rest as arbitrary impositions. The context of abtar in verse 3, apparently one whose lineage ends and who has no progeny, makes the primary sense abundant progeny; alternatively, it is abundant good generally, including descendants, since otherwise the inversion in the final verse fails. The plural “We,” Indeed, and iʿṭāʾ express God’s greatness, favour, a grant of ownership, and comfort to the Prophet. The verse implies that Fāṭimah’s children count as his lineage, and forecasts their multiplication despite their persecution and frequent massacre.
verses.2: Al-Mizan treats the fāʾ as making prayer and inḥar the grateful consequence of the gift of kawthar. Sunni and Shia narrations from the Prophet and Imam ʿAlī, together with Shia narrations from Imam al-Ṣādiq and other Imams, interpret naḥr here as raising the hands to the neck when saying Allāh akbar in ritual prayer. Other suggested views are the Eid prayer with a camel offering, or standing upright after rukūʿ and raising one’s head.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines shāniʾ as mubghiḍ—an enemy, opponent, or one who dislikes another—and al-abtar as one without children. It identifies the insulter as al-ʿĀṣ b. Wāʾil. The alternatives “cut off from all good” and “cut off from his people” would make the verse a reversal against him, but the commentary says they conflict with mustafiḍah narrations. Those narrations connect the revelation with someone mocking the Prophet as childless after the deaths of his sons Qāsim and ʿAbd-Allāh.
